title: Ceylon gains independence from Britain
description: Ceylon became an independent dominion within the British Commonwealth on 4 February 1948, with Don Stephen Senanayake as the first Prime Minister. The transfer of power was negotiated peacefully, maintaining defence and economic ties with Britain. Independence set the stage for decades of political competition between English-educated elites and vernacular nationalist movements.

title: Indian Tamils stripped of citizenship and voting rights
description: The Indian and Pakistani Residents (Citizenship) Act of 1949 rendered hundreds of thousands of Indian Tamil plantation workers stateless and disenfranchised by 1950. The policy stripped a large segment of the workforce of political voice and civil rights. It set an early precedent for ethnically discriminatory legislation that deepened communal tensions over subsequent decades.

title: Ceylon Freedom Party founded by S.W.R.D. Bandaranaike
description: Solomon Bandaranaike broke from the ruling United National Party to establish the Ceylon Freedom Party (SLFP), a centre-left nationalist party championing Sinhala Buddhist interests. The SLFP's founding reshaped Ceylonese politics and created the two-party rivalry that would dominate the country for decades. It became the political vehicle for Sinhala vernacular nationalism.

title: Hartal general strike paralyses Ceylon over rice subsidies
description: A nationwide general strike erupted in August 1953 in protest against the removal of a rice subsidy, coordinated by left-wing parties including the LSSP and the Communist Party. The government declared a state of emergency and Prime Minister Dudley Senanayake resigned citing ill health and the political storm. The Hartal demonstrated the power of organised labour and left-wing politics in early Ceylon.

title: Ceylon signs rubber-rice barter agreement with China
description: Ceylon concluded a landmark barter agreement with the People's Republic of China, exchanging rubber for rice, which secured affordable food staples and a market for plantation rubber. The deal drew criticism from the United States, which maintained trade restrictions on China. It signalled Ceylon's willingness to engage pragmatically across Cold War lines.

title: Sinhala Only Act passed — landmark language flashpoint
description: Prime Minister S.W.R.D. Bandaranaike passed the Official Language Act making Sinhala the sole official language, winning the 1956 election on a Sinhala nationalist platform. Tamil leaders staged a nonviolent protest on the Galle Face Green and were attacked by Sinhala mobs, marking the first major ethnic riots. The act alienated the Tamil community and is widely seen as the turning point that set Ceylon on the path toward communal conflict.

title: Bandaranaike-Chelvanayakam Pact signed then abrogated
description: Prime Minister Bandaranaike and Tamil Federal Party leader Chelvanayakam signed a pact granting reasonable use of Tamil in administrative affairs and some regional autonomy. The agreement was abrogated the following year under pressure from Sinhala nationalists and UNP opposition leader Dudley Senanayake. Its failure deepened Tamil political disillusionment and foreclosed an early chance for ethnic compromise.

title: Anti-Tamil riots kill hundreds across Ceylon
description: Widespread anti-Tamil communal violence erupted in May 1958, leaving hundreds dead and tens of thousands displaced following the abrogation of the Bandaranaike-Chelvanayakam Pact. A state of emergency was declared and curfews imposed, but the violence marked a traumatic escalation of ethnic tension. The 1958 riots became a reference point for the cycles of communal violence that followed.

title: Prime Minister Bandaranaike assassinated by Buddhist monk
description: S.W.R.D. Bandaranaike was shot at his home in Colombo on 25 September 1959 by Buddhist monk Talduwe Somarama, linked to extremist groups who felt Bandaranaike had betrayed their cause. He died the following day, plunging Ceylon into political uncertainty. The killing shocked the country and paved the way for his widow Sirimavo to enter politics.

title: Sirimavo Bandaranaike becomes world's first female PM
description: Sirimavo Bandaranaike, widow of the assassinated premier, led the SLFP to victory in the July 1960 elections and was sworn in as Prime Minister, becoming the world's first female head of government. Her government continued the SLFP's nationalist and socialist agenda including further nationalisation. She proved a formidable politician and served multiple terms over three decades.

title: Tamil Federal Party launches civil disobedience in the north
description: The Tamil Federal Party launched a major civil disobedience campaign demanding federal autonomy and recognition of Tamil as an official language, with demonstrators occupying government offices in Jaffna. The government declared a state of emergency and deployed the military to the north. The episode marked an early militarisation of the ethnic dispute.

title: Nationalisation of Western oil companies triggers US aid cutoff
description: The government nationalised assets of Caltex, Shell, and Esso, creating the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation, and the move generated a US aid cutoff under the Hickenlooper Amendment. Ceylon sought and received alternative assistance from the Soviet Union and other socialist states. The episode illustrated the Cold War dimensions of economic nationalism in small developing states.

title: Sirimavo-Shastri Pact on stateless Indian Tamil workers
description: Ceylon and India signed an agreement allocating 525,000 stateless plantation workers to Indian citizenship and 300,000 to Ceylon citizenship, with 150,000 left for later negotiation. Implementation proved slow and contentious, leaving many workers in legal limbo for years. The pact was a landmark but ultimately incomplete resolution of a post-independence humanitarian problem.

title: First JVP insurrection — Marxist youth uprising suppressed
description: The Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna (JVP), a Marxist youth movement led by Rohana Wijeweera, launched a coordinated armed insurrection in April 1971, attacking police stations and government installations across the country. Thousands of young Sinhalese disillusioned by unemployment and inequality participated before the uprising was suppressed with significant loss of life. JVP leader Wijeweera and thousands of cadres were arrested.

title: Ceylon becomes Republic of Sri Lanka under new constitution
description: A new republican constitution came into force on 22 May 1972, changing the country's name from Ceylon to Sri Lanka and severing the link with the British Crown. The constitution gave Buddhism the foremost place among religions and entrenched Sinhala as the official language, deepening Tamil alienation. Sri Lanka became a republic within the Commonwealth but no longer a dominion.

title: Standardisation policy restricts Tamil university admissions
description: The government introduced a standardisation policy requiring Tamil students to score higher than Sinhalese students for university admission in science and engineering, effectively reducing Tamil representation. Tamils had historically been over-represented in these fields due to English-medium education. The policy radicalised a generation of Tamil youth who felt systematically excluded from professional advancement.

title: Jaffna Mayor Duraiappah assassinated by Prabhakaran
description: Alfred Duraiappah, the Tamil Mayor of Jaffna and SLFP supporter, was assassinated by Velupillai Prabhakaran in July 1975 in his first known public act of violence. The killing marked the beginning of targeted political assassinations by Tamil militants and signalled a shift toward armed struggle within the Tamil movement. It was the opening act of what would become the LTTE's campaign.

title: UNP wins landslide; anti-Tamil riots erupt nationwide
description: Junius Richard Jayewardene led the United National Party to an overwhelming electoral victory in July 1977, taking 140 of 168 parliamentary seats. In the weeks following the election, widespread anti-Tamil violence erupted in parts of southern and central Sri Lanka, leaving dozens dead and thousands displaced. The riots further eroded Tamil faith in the state's willingness to protect minorities.

title: New executive presidential constitution enacted
description: A new constitution came into force in September 1978, creating a powerful French-style executive presidency. J.R. Jayewardene became the first executive president of Sri Lanka, and the constitution concentrated power in the presidency. It was accompanied by sweeping economic liberalisation, opening Sri Lanka to foreign investment and establishing Export Processing Zones.

title: Prevention of Terrorism Act grants sweeping security powers
description: The government enacted the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA), granting security forces sweeping powers to detain suspects without charge for extended periods, primarily targeting Tamil militant groups. The law was criticised by human rights organisations as enabling arbitrary detention and torture. The PTA became a lasting and controversial tool of counterinsurgency used across successive governments.

title: Jaffna Public Library burned — 97,000 books destroyed
description: In June 1981, the Jaffna Public Library was set on fire by Sinhala police and paramilitary personnel, destroying approximately 97,000 books and irreplaceable Tamil manuscripts. The burning was a catastrophic act of cultural destruction that enraged Tamils across Sri Lanka and the diaspora. It became an enduring symbol of state-sponsored violence against Tamil heritage and drove many Tamils toward support for the LTTE.

title: Black July — anti-Tamil pogrom kills thousands
description: In July 1983, following an LTTE ambush that killed 13 soldiers, anti-Tamil riots erupted across Colombo with mobs using electoral rolls to systematically target Tamil homes and businesses, killing an estimated 400 to 3,000 people. Evidence of state complicity — including the participation of ruling-party politicians — caused permanent damage to Sinhalese-Tamil relations. Black July accelerated the Tamil exodus to the diaspora and effectively marked the start of the civil war.

title: Civil war begins; LTTE emerges as dominant Tamil armed group
description: Black July triggered the formal beginning of Sri Lanka's civil war as Tamil youth flocked to militant organisations in unprecedented numbers after the pogrom. The LTTE systematically eliminated rival Tamil organisations, emerging as the most ruthless and disciplined armed group. India began covertly training and arming Tamil militant groups, including the LTTE, at this stage.

title: Indo-Sri Lanka Accord and Indian peacekeeping force deployed
description: As the Sri Lankan military mounted a major offensive against LTTE strongholds, India brokered the Indo-Sri Lanka Accord in July 1987 and deployed the Indian Peace Keeping Force to disarm the LTTE. The 13th Amendment to the constitution established provincial councils and made Tamil an official language alongside Sinhala. Both the LTTE and Sinhala nationalists opposed the accord, and the IPKF quickly became embroiled in fighting the LTTE.

title: Second JVP insurrection terrorises southern Sri Lanka
description: The JVP, reconstituted and radicalised, launched a second insurrection in the Sinhalese south in 1988-89, targeting the UNP government and anyone perceived as collaborating with the Indian presence. JVP death squads assassinated politicians, trade unionists, and civil servants, while the government's counter-insurgency killed thousands. The violence paralysed southern Sri Lanka for two years before leader Wijeweera was captured and killed in November 1989.

title: LTTE expels 75,000 Muslims from Northern Province
description: In October 1990, the LTTE gave the Muslim population of the Northern Province approximately 48 hours to leave, forcibly expelling an estimated 75,000 people from their homes. The expulsion was carried out with extreme brutality and the displaced Muslims lost homes, land, and livelihoods. The act was widely condemned and deepened Muslim-Tamil divisions, creating a displaced community that remained unable to return for decades.

title: LTTE suicide bomber assassinates Indian PM Rajiv Gandhi
description: A female LTTE suicide bomber assassinated former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi at an election rally in Tamil Nadu on 21 May 1991, attributed to Gandhi's decision to send the IPKF against the LTTE. The killing turned India firmly against the LTTE, ending any residual Indian sympathy for the Tamil militant cause. The assassination had profound consequences for India-Sri Lanka relations and the diplomatic landscape of the conflict.

title: President Premadasa assassinated by LTTE suicide bomber
description: President Ranasinghe Premadasa was killed by an LTTE suicide bomber at a May Day political rally in Colombo on 1 May 1993, demonstrating the LTTE's ability to strike at the highest levels of government. The assassination of a sitting head of state shocked the country and led Prime Minister D.B. Wijetunga to succeed him. It marked the height of LTTE urban terrorism in the capital.

title: Kumaratunga elected on peace platform; talks collapse
description: Chandrika Kumaratunga won presidential elections in November 1994 campaigning on a peace initiative, with her mother Sirimavo Bandaranaike returning as Prime Minister. The talks with the LTTE collapsed in April 1995 after the LTTE sank two navy vessels and withdrew from the ceasefire. The failure led to Eelam War III, which saw some of the most intense fighting of the conflict.

title: Military captures Jaffna city from LTTE in Operation Riviresa
description: The Sri Lankan military launched Operation Riviresa and recaptured the Jaffna Peninsula from LTTE control in late 1995, a major military and symbolic victory. Hundreds of thousands of Tamil civilians fled the peninsula in the weeks before and during the offensive. The recapture of Jaffna was celebrated in the south but came with a massive humanitarian displacement.

title: LTTE truck bomb destroys Central Bank — 91 killed
description: A massive LTTE truck bomb exploded outside the Central Bank of Sri Lanka in Colombo on 31 January 1996, killing 91 people and injuring over 1,400. The bombing caused enormous economic damage and disrupted the financial sector for weeks. It was one of the deadliest single attacks of the civil war and demonstrated the LTTE's devastating capacity for urban terrorism.

title: LTTE attacks Bandaranaike Airport — $350M economic damage
description: A combined LTTE suicide squad attacked Bandaranaike International Airport and the adjoining air force base in July 2001, destroying or damaging much of Sri Lanka's civilian fleet and military aircraft. The attack caused an estimated $350 million in economic damage and sent insurance and aviation costs soaring. It was the single most economically damaging attack of the civil war.

title: Norway-facilitated Ceasefire Agreement signed with LTTE
description: The government and LTTE signed a Norwegian-facilitated Ceasefire Agreement in February 2002, ending active hostilities and opening the A9 highway to civilian traffic for the first time in years. The ceasefire brought an immediate and dramatic improvement in living conditions in the north and east and formal peace talks began in Thailand. It was the most serious peace initiative of the civil war.

title: Indian Ocean tsunami kills 35,000 Sri Lankans
description: The catastrophic Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004 struck Sri Lanka's southern, eastern, and northern coastlines, killing approximately 35,000 people and displacing over one million. Entire coastal communities were wiped out, fishing industries destroyed, and critical infrastructure obliterated. Sri Lanka suffered one of the highest death tolls of any country affected by the disaster.

title: Karuna faction splits from LTTE, weakening eastern wing
description: Colonel Karuna, the LTTE's eastern military commander, defected from the organisation in March 2004 with thousands of fighters, splitting the organisation and weakening its eastern wing. The government eventually incorporated Karuna's forces as a paramilitary group. The defection significantly altered the military balance in the Eastern Province and contributed to the government's eventual success in clearing the east.

title: Rajapaksa elected president on Sinhala nationalist platform
description: Mahinda Rajapaksa won the November 2005 presidential election by a narrow margin after the LTTE effectively boycotted the poll in northern areas, running on a nationalist platform opposing federal solutions. His election marked a decisive shift away from the peace process approach of the Wickremesinghe government. It opened the path to the final military push to defeat the LTTE.

title: LTTE defeated; 26-year civil war ends in military victory
description: The Sri Lankan military defeated the LTTE in a final offensive in May 2009, killing LTTE leader Velupillai Prabhakaran and most of the senior leadership in the Nanthikadal lagoon area on 18-19 May. The 26-year civil war ended with a decisive government military victory, but UN estimates suggest tens of thousands of Tamil civilians may have died in the final offensive. The end of the war was celebrated by Sinhala nationalists but condemned by Tamil diaspora groups and international human rights organisations.

title: 300,000 Tamil civilians held in internment camps post-war
description: Following the end of the war, approximately 300,000 Tamil civilians who had been caught in the conflict zone were held in internment camps in harsh conditions with severely restricted humanitarian access. The conditions attracted widespread international criticism and calls for accountability. The mass displacement represented one of the largest forced detentions in post-war Asia.

title: 18th Amendment removes presidential term limits
description: The 18th Amendment to the constitution was passed by the Rajapaksa government, removing the two-term limit on the presidency and weakening independent commissions for the judiciary, police, and civil service. Sri Lanka began a trajectory toward democratic backsliding under the Rajapaksa family. The amendment was seen by opposition parties and civil society as a dangerous concentration of executive power.

title: Chief Justice impeached in assault on judicial independence
description: Chief Justice Shirani Bandaranayake was impeached by a parliamentary select committee dominated by the ruling party after she delivered rulings unfavourable to the government. The Supreme Court ruled the impeachment process unconstitutional but the government proceeded regardless. The episode was widely seen as a serious assault on judicial independence and drew international condemnation.

title: Hambantota Port leased to China — debt trap controversy
description: Sri Lanka's Hambantota Port, built with Chinese loans, was operational and the government entered further agreements with Chinese state enterprises for a surrounding industrial zone. The accumulation of Chinese debt secured on infrastructure assets began attracting international scrutiny. The port deal would later force a 99-year lease to China Merchants Port Holdings in 2017, becoming a globally cited example of debt-trap diplomacy.

title: Sirisena defeats Rajapaksa; democratic reforms restored
description: Maithripala Sirisena, a defector from the Rajapaksa cabinet, won a surprise presidential election victory in January 2015, defeating the incumbent Mahinda Rajapaksa on a platform of good governance and anti-corruption. The National Unity Government subsequently passed the 19th Amendment, restoring the two-term presidential limit and strengthening independent commissions. The result was celebrated internationally as a restoration of democratic norms.

title: Constitutional crisis as president sacks PM illegally
description: President Sirisena dismissed Prime Minister Wickremesinghe in October 2018 and attempted to replace him with Mahinda Rajapaksa, provoking a constitutional crisis. The Supreme Court ruled the dissolution of parliament unconstitutional and Wickremesinghe was eventually reinstated after weeks of political chaos. The crisis exposed deep fractures in the national unity government and damaged democratic institutions.

title: Easter Sunday bombings kill 269 — worst attack since civil war
description: On Easter Sunday, 21 April 2019, coordinated suicide bombings by National Thowheed Jamath, linked to ISIS, struck three luxury hotels and three churches in Colombo, Negombo, and Batticaloa, killing 269 people and injuring over 500. The attack caused an immediate collapse of tourism and triggered major political controversy over intelligence failures despite prior warnings. It was the deadliest terrorist attack in Sri Lanka's post-war history.

title: Gotabaya Rajapaksa elected president on security platform
description: Gotabaya Rajapaksa, former defence secretary and brother of Mahinda, won the presidential election in November 2019 exploiting public anxiety over security after the Easter bombings. He won with 52 percent of the vote on a platform of Sinhala Buddhist nationalism and development. His election restored the Rajapaksa family to power and raised concerns among Tamil and Muslim minorities.

title: Overnight organic farming ban causes agricultural collapse
description: President Gotabaya Rajapaksa implemented an overnight ban on chemical fertilisers and pesticides, ordering Sri Lanka to convert entirely to organic farming without adequate preparation or alternatives. Catastrophic crop failures followed in rice, tea, and other key crops, and Sri Lanka was forced to import food, deepening the foreign exchange crisis. The policy was reversed within months after causing severe food insecurity.

title: Economic collapse — sovereign default and 50% inflation
description: Sri Lanka experienced its most severe economic crisis since independence in 2022, characterised by a sovereign debt default, foreign exchange depletion, inflation exceeding 50 percent, and severe shortages of fuel, medicine, cooking gas, and food. Power cuts of up to 13 hours daily were imposed. The crisis was the product of accumulated debt, tax cuts, pandemic shocks, the fertiliser ban, and systematic governance failures.

title: Aragalaya protests force Gotabaya Rajapaksa from power
description: Millions of Sri Lankans participated in the Aragalaya (struggle) mass protests demanding the Rajapaksa government's resignation, culminating on 9 July 2022 when hundreds of thousands stormed the Presidential Secretariat and PM's residence. President Gotabaya Rajapaksa fled to the Maldives and resigned on 13 July 2022, the first Sri Lankan president forced from office by popular protest. The movement was spontaneous, leaderless, and crossed ethnic and class lines.

title: Parliament elects Wickremesinghe president to manage IMF talks
description: Parliament elected Ranil Wickremesinghe as president in July 2022 to complete Gotabaya Rajapaksa's term, given his technical capacity to manage IMF negotiations. His election was opposed by Aragalaya activists who viewed him as a continuation of the political establishment. He immediately began austerity measures and formal IMF negotiations.

title: IMF approves $2.9 billion bailout for Sri Lanka
description: The International Monetary Fund's executive board approved a $2.9 billion Extended Fund Facility for Sri Lanka in March 2023, the country's largest ever IMF programme. The programme required substantial fiscal adjustment, central bank reforms, and a credible debt restructuring process. Sri Lanka also reached restructuring agreements with bilateral creditors including India, China, and the Paris Club.

title: AKD wins presidency — first non-UNP/SLFP leader since independence
description: Anura Kumara Dissanayake of the left-nationalist National People's Power coalition won the September 2024 presidential election, becoming the first president from outside the UNP-SLFP establishment since independence. His NPP subsequently won a commanding parliamentary majority in November 2024, the most dramatic political realignment in post-independence history. He promised anti-corruption governance while continuing the IMF programme.

title: Sri Lanka Wins 1996 Cricket World Cup as Co-Host
description: Sri Lanka defeated Australia by seven wickets in the 1996 Cricket World Cup final on March 17, 1996 at Gaddafi Stadium in Lahore, Pakistan, with Aravinda de Silva scoring an unbeaten 107 and taking 3 wickets to win Player of the Match. Co-hosting the tournament with India and Pakistan, Sri Lanka became the first host nation ever to win the Cricket World Cup. The triumph, led by captain Arjuna Ranatunga, transformed Sri Lanka into a cricketing powerhouse and a source of major national pride.
